text: In immuno- competent individuals, acute pulmonary disease is usually mild and self-limiting and in 60% of cases resolves with- out specific chemotherapy. In some patients the infection progresses to chronic pulmonary coccidioidomycosis with granulomatous lesions, fibrosis, and cavitation. Less than 1% of patients develop acute progressive pneumonia (which is commonly fatal if untreated) or disseminated disease (usually involving the skin, bone, meninges, and joints). Severe pulmonary and disseminated infections are more likely in pregnant women, males, certain ethnic groups, diabetics, and immunocompromised patients. Treatment is usually reserved for severe, progressive, or disseminated infections or for patients with concurrent risk factors, especially immunosuppression.1,2 If antifungal therapy is given, it is preferably with an oral azole as initial therapy or with intravenous amphotericin B;1,3 itracona- zole and fluconazole are used most often, while voricona- zole has been reported to be effective in some patients who have not responded to fluconazole.4 Amphotericin B is generally used for rapidly progressive disease while azoles are generally preferred for chronic disease.1,2 Although combination therapy with an azole and amphotericin B has been used, there is no evidence that it is superior to a single antifungal drug.1 Diffuse pneumonia is most often seen in immunocompromised patients and treatment is initially with an azole or amphotericin B followed by maintenance treatment with an azole for a year or more. In immuno- compromised patients it is advisable to continue treatment indefinitely.4 Fluconazole is effective in meningeal infec- tions and is the most frequently recommended antifungal for this indication,1,2,4 although itraconazole has also pro- duced beneficial responses; intrathecal amphotericin B may also be used, especially in aggressive infections.1,2,5 Due to the high incidence of relapse, indefinite suppres- sive therapy with fluconazole or itraconazole is recom- mended for patients with coccidioidal meningitis or dif- fuse pulmonary coccidioidomycosis.1 Patients with HIV infection and solid organ transplant recipients who have completed induction therapy should subsequently receive lifelong suppressive fluconazole or itraconazole.2,6,7 It may, however, be possible to stop therapy in patients with CD4+ lymphocyte counts above 250 cells/microlitre (ex- cept in those with meningitis) if there is clinical evidence that the coccidioidal infection is controlled.1 Primary prophylaxis for HIV-infected patients living in coccidioid- omycosis-endemic areas is not routinely recommended.1,6 However, primary prophylaxis may be considered for sol- id organ transplant recipients who are at risk of coccidioi- dal infection.1,7 1.
